Copper-Catalyzed Three-Component Carboboronation of Allenes
Using Highly Strained Cyclic Ketimines as Electrophiles
Hao Deng,# Yujie Dong,# Yu Shangguan, Fazhou Yang, Sheng Han, Jiaqi Wu, Bo Liang, Hongchao Guo,
and Cheng Zhang *
Cite This: Org. Lett. 2021, 23, 4431 −4435 Read Online
ACCESS Metrics & More Article Recommendations *sı Supporting Information
ABSTRACT: A diastereoselective copper and NHC-ligand-catalyzed three-component difunctionalization of allenes with
bis(pinacolato)diboron and 2 H-azirines to a ﬀord borylated allylaziridines is described. The reaction exhibits complete
diastereoselectivity and good yields, and the further chlorination of the corresponding borylated products was also performed. It
is believed that the high ring-strain force of 2 H-azirines facilitates the reaction. More chemical transformations of borylated
allylaziridines are also reported.
B
oron-containing compounds play important roles in
organic synthesis, 1a,b catalysis, 1c−e materials, 1f,g and
therapeutic drug discovery. 1h Therefore, the development of
eﬃcient methods to obtain such compounds is highly
desirable. Among various methods to acquire them, the
transition-metal-catalyzed borylative difunctionalization of
unsaturated hydrocarbons is highly attractive because it usually
aﬀords multifunctional boron-containing products, which are
favorable building blocks in organic synthesis.
2 Copper has
been found to be the most attractive catalyst for such
reactions.3 In a typical reaction pathway, the boron-containing
organocopper species is formed in situ via the addition of
borylcopper to alkenes, alkynes, or allenes, which would then
undergo nucleophilic additions or substitutions with electro-
philes.
3e However, unlike organocuprates (organocopperate
complex),4 the in situ-generated boron-substituted organo-
copper species exhibit a unique nucleophilic reactivity since
only speciﬁc electrophiles are suitable substrates. For example,
the allylcopper species
3a−c could undergo nucleophilic
reactions with a few types of halides, 5 allyl esters, 6 ketones,
aldehydes,7 imines,8 highly electron-de ﬁcient alkenes, 9 and
other electrophiles. 10
When imines are used as the electrophiles, the correspond-
ing products of their reaction with the allylcopper species are
boron-substituted homoallylic amines, which are important
intermediates to synthesize natural products and bioactive
molecules. Therefore, reactions with allylcopper species that
employ imines as electrophiles attract considerable attention
(Scheme 1 ).
11 Aldimines were ﬁrst used as electrophilic
reaction partners in the three-component carboboronation of
allenes with bis(pinacolato)diboron (B
2Pin2) by Procter. 8a,b
However, ketimines have proven to be much more challenging
substrates than aldimines for the reaction until Hoveyda made
a breakthrough by utilizing unprotected ketimine salts as the
electrophiles, and the nitrogen atom bearing a positive charge
makes the ketimine salts more prone to an attack by the
nucleophilic organocopper species.
8g Very recently, Procter
reported that ketiminoesters are also favorable substrates for
the boron-containing allylcopper species because the electron-
withdrawing ester group activates the ketimines.
8c
Our group is interested in employing cyclic imines as
electrophiles in the copper-catalyzed carboboronation of
allenes and has developed a copper-catalyzed enantioselective
carboboronation reaction of allenes using seven-membered
cyclic aldimines as electrophiles.
12 However, when seven-
membered cyclic ketimines were subjected to the reaction, no
desired product was detected. We then wondered whether
highly strained three-membered cyclic ketimines could be

active enough to be attacked by the in situ-formed boron-
substituted allylcopper species. 13 As a result, we report here a
copper-catalyzed carboboronation of allenes with diboronates
and 2 H-azirines.
Initially, we selected the reaction of 2,3-diphenyl-2 H-azirine
1a, phenyl allene 2a, and bis(pinacolato)diboron 3 as the
model reaction. Then, we probed a series of copper salts,
ligands, bases, solvents, temperatures, and loading ratios of
substrates to obtain the optimal reaction conditions ( Table 1).
To our delight, the desired product 4aa was obtained in a 76%
yield and >20:1 dr in the presence of 10 mol % CuCl and 15
mol % IPrNHC using
tBuOK as the base and PhCF 3 as the
solvent at room temperature ( Table 1, entry 1), and the crystal
structure of product 4aa was unambiguously identi ﬁed.
However, an evaluation of other ligands (such as DPPF,
DPPBz, bipy, et al.) indicated that P,P- and N,N-ligands
impaired the reaction yield remarkably, and IPrNHC was still
the best ligand ( Table 1 , entries 2 −4, respectively). Switching
tBuOK to other bases, such as tBuONa, tBuOLi, and MeOK,
resulted in lower yields of 4aa (Table 1 , entries 5 −7,
respectively). We then screened several other copper salts,
including CuBr, CuI, Cu(OAc)
2, Cu(OTf)2, and CuBr2 (Table
1, entries 8−12, resptively). Among them, Cu(OAc) 2 exhibited
the best performance, and product 4aa was obtained in an 83%
yield ( Table 1 , entry 10). Examinations of di ﬀerent solvents
indicated that PhCF3 was still the best solvent ( Table 1, entries
13−15). Both elevating and decreasing the reaction temper-
ature was harmful to the reaction, since lower yields of 4aa
were obtained ( Table 1 , entries 16 and 17). The loading ratio
of the copper salt to the ligand had a huge e ﬀect on the
reaction, since the yield of 4aa was greatly decreased when a
1:1 ratio of Cu(OAc) 2/IPrNHC was used as the catalyst
(Table 1 , entry 18).
After the optimal conditions were obtained, we set out to
evaluate the performance of various substituted 2 H-azirine 1
and allenes 2 for the reaction. It was found that most of the
boronated products 4 were di ﬃcult to be characterized by
NMR (nuclear magnetic resonance) spectroscopy due to bad
signal splitting in the
1H NMR spectrum and missing signals in
the 13C NMR spectrum. 14 Therefore, all of them were then
converted to chlorinated products 5 using CuCl 2 as the
chlorine source for a better NMR analysis, and the yields of 4
and total yields of 5 in two steps are reported in Tables 2 and
3, respectively. Complete diastereoselectivity was obtained for
all the reactions.
For all the allene substrates, the corresponding products
were obtained with moderate to good yields. For arylallenes,
alkyl-substituted phenylallenes ( Table 2, entries 2 −4) aﬀorded
the corresponding products with lower yields than those from
halogen- or oxygen-substituted phenylallenes ( Table 2 , entries
5−7, respectively). Noticeably, the CF
3-substituted phenyl-
allene 2h aﬀorded the corresponding product 5ah in a
considerablely low yield ( Table 2 , entry 8). Additionally,
allenes with substituents at di ﬀerent positions of the phenyl
ring exhibited similar reactivities under the optimal conditions,
and the desired products were obtained in 68% −75% total
yields ( Table 2 , entries 9 −12). However, alkylallene 5m
exhibited a much weaker reactivity than those of the phenyl
allenes , and the corresponding boronated product was
obtained in a 36% yield. ( Table 2 , entry 13). To further
expand the scope of the allene substrates, other types of

allenes, such as α-substituted phenylallene 2n, phenoxylallene
2o, and allenamide 2p, were also subjected to the optimal
reaction conditions. Unfortunately, none of them were suitable
substrates for the reaction since no desired products was
detected.
The substrate scope of 2 H-Azirines was then evaluated, and
substrates with variations on both R
1 and R 2 groups were
examined under the standard conditions. When R 1 and R 2
were substituted phenyl groups, little in ﬂuence on product
yields was observed. When R 2 was a phenyl group, the
substrates bearing substituents with di ﬀerent electronic
properties (Me, nPr, and Cl) on the para-position of phenyl
rings a ﬀorded good yields of the desired products ( Table 3 ,
entries 1 −3, respectively). Similarly, When R 1 was a phenyl
group, the corresponding products were obtained in high
yields regardless of the presence of alkyl or halogen
substituents or their substituted positions on phenyl rings of
R
2. However, when R 1 was H, no desired product was
obtained, and we found that the substrate decomposed rapidly
under standard conditions.
Followed by the expansion of substrate scope, a scaled-up
synthesis of 4aa was then evaluated. When the reaction of 1a
was scaled up to 1 mmol (based on 1a) under the optimal
conditions, 4aa was obtained in a 61% yield, which is
considerably lower than that in a smaller-scale synthesis.
However, the yield for the chlorination reaction remained
almost the same ( Scheme 2.1). In addition to the chlorination
of the boryl group in product 4, more transformations of the
boryl group were tried. The protection of the amine group can
be achieved by reacting compound 4a with benzoyl chloride in
the presence of Et
3N and DMAP using DCM as the solvent,
and the protected product 4aa underwent a paladium-catalyzed
cross-coupling reaction with iodobenzene in a 70% yield over
two steps ( Scheme 2.2a). The protected product could also be
converted to the corresponding ketone 7 in a 74% yield in two
steps via a typical oxidative workup process ( Scheme 2 .2b)
(Scheme 2 (1)). The asymmetric version of the synthesis of
compound 4aa was also investigated. However, only a poor
yield and a moderate enantioselecvitity were obtained. 15
In summary, we have developed a copper-catalyzed three-
component carboboronation of arylallenes using 2 H-azirines as
the electrophiles. It shows that such highly strained three-
membered ketimines with diverse substituents are suitable
substrates, aﬀording the corresponding products in good yields
and with complete diastereoselectivity. Additionally, the
products were further converted to chlorinated products in
good yields. More chemical transformations of borylated
allylaziridines were also described.
